newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Rugby sees more job losses in 97.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Rugby sees more job losses in 97.

text.p: Rugby Group Plc, the UK building materials firm, warned on Thursday that its restructuring process was not over yet and predicted further job losses this year on top of those already announced.

Peter Johnson, group chief executive, said in an interview: "The process is not completed. There could be further rationalisation of jobs." But he would not go any further. Rugby has already announced 535 job cuts, which taking into account the creation of new jobs, leaves a net loss of 370.

The group has already begun the restructuring in some units including the UK business John Carr and is in the process of integrating Boulton and Paul. Changes are underway at Rugby Building Products and Stegbar.

Johnson said the U.S. distribution business, RBP,in particular needed more action. Rugby announced earlier the appointment of Stephen Brown as president of the unit. Brown is set to speed up the cost cutting and margin improvement.

Asked where 1997 growth would come from -- bearing in mind the restructuring, the European market is far from buoyant and the U.S. market is unlikely to match 1996's peak -- he said that the benefits of the Rugby shake-up would feed through by the year-end.
He added that Rugby was erring on the side of caution in its statement, not wishing to repeat the mistakes of the sector last year when upbeat statements were followed by profit warnings later.

"We expect some of the results of restructuring to come through in 1997, with substantial progress being made next year." Rugby said the start to 1997 was promising, with volumes in UK cement up "not far off 10 percent in the first 10 weeks."
In joinery, the volume growth was more than 10 percent, he said. But he added that these figures were compared to a very low base last year, when the industry was hit by poor weather conditions.

On the subject of whether shareholders will see dividend growth this year, he said "Historically we see dividend cover of two (times) as sensible over the cycle. Our object is to improve profits and get it growing again when it's prudent to do so." He did not expect profits in 1997 to be hit by additional charges on top of the 10 million hit from the sale of ZND. That will be partially offset by a small profit form the sale of UK metal units, he said.
